newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia acts to boost confidence in property markets.
newsitem.headline: Asia acts to boost confidence in property markets.

text.p: Asian governments, faced with dislocations in local property markets, are tapping a variety of financial measures to restore investor confidence and safeguard a sector that has been a powerhouse of economic growth.

Thailand most recently opened its market to foreigners to try to reduce the glut of unsold properties, while Malaysia and the Philippines put a limit on property loans by banks financial institutions to limit their exposure.
Hong Kong, meanwhile, imposed curbs to stem excessive speculation in an undersupplied property market as it gears up for its handover to China at the end of June.
Many officials and economists believe the measures may be insufficient to rectify all the problems, but agree that without them investor confidence would have been lost.

"The spirit of the regulations is not to plug all loopholes," Bank Negara's Deputy Governor, Fong Weng Phak, said recently of measures Malaysia introduced to avert a repetition of the speculative bubble that afflicts Thailand.
Instead, he said "the spirit is to send a message to the country about...preventing a build-up of an asset bubble."
How successful the measures will be remains to be seen and will depend to a great extent on the local environment.
Japan has been struggling with its troubled real estate markets for some seven years, while Thailand's problems came to a head last year and remain unsettled.
Recently, all eyes have been on the Philippines, where the stock market has been savaged by fears of a Thai-style property melt-down.
Over the past few days, Manila's share index has fallen more than 20 percent below its record high in February in a wave of selling described by many dealers as a bloodbath.
Still, those stepping back from the debacle say the Philippines cannot be compared to Thailand.
"Real estate here has not been financed by foreign loans (like Thailand)," said Teresa Paningco, an economist at the University of Asia and the Pacific.
She said that while the Central Bank's moves to curb lending to the property sector suggested some caution was warranted, the concerns were not significant enough to cause a collapse.
By contrast, Thailand is struggling with a mountain of unsold properties, billions of baht in bad loans and a slowing economy.
Some analysts believe the situation in Thailand could drag on for at least two years because of the huge overhang of problem loans.
"It's going to get worse for bank and finance companies as the proportion of non-performing loans rises," said Philip Sheridan, a property analyst at Thaimex Finance and Securities.
With Thailand as a backdrop, analysts say it is not surprising other markets have reacted so dramatically to rumours that some of their major property firms are in big trouble.
Dynamic econcomic growth has enabled Asia's emerging economies to capture the attention -- and investment dollars -- of the international financial markets.
If that growth slows, so do the prospects for the profitable returns that have rewarded investors for risks they have taken.
Thailand's stock market was ravaged as investment funds and private investors salvaged whatever they could as the economic scenario deteriorated.
So far, the outlook for economic growth in the region does not appear dire.
The Philippines government is expecting growth of up to eight percent this year, compared to 6.8 percent in 1996, which was it's highest in six years.
Economists say even if growth is somewhat lower, it would still be strong enough to produce healthy corporate profits.
Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, looks for growth of around eight percent this year compared with nine percent in the last few years.

"Definitely you will see some economic slowdown (due to the property glut)...Bank Negara's curb is to remove speculation and move up growth after 1999," said Phua Lee Kerk, head of research at Jupiter Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
In Singapore, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong warned in his May Day message against overbuilding and the impact it could have on the economy.
"If we overbuild properties to satisfy get-rich-quick demand...the property market may collapse, causing serious problems for the whole economy," Goh said.
Singapore stocks were hard hit earlier this week by rumours the government would hold a weekend news conference to announce it would impose further restrictions on the property market.
A Ministry of National Development said on Tuesday he was not aware of any plans for such a news conference and property stocks recovered.
